newsitem.title: UK: Fishermen end UK oil blockade but vow to fight on.
newsitem.headline: Fishermen end UK oil blockade but vow to fight on.

text.p: Shetland fishermen abandoned their blockade of Britain's biggest oil port on Tuesday but vowed to keep up their fight for compensation following the Braer tanker spill four years ago.
Fourteen shell fishing boats blocked access to the giant Sullom Voe export terminal for a day and a half before heading home on Tuesday afternoon.
"We've been told by the police and the harbour master that if we didn't move we'd be fined," said Sidney Johnson aboard the prawn dredger "Aquarius".
"But we'll keep fighting and do it again if we have to" he added.
The crews were protesting against a lack of compensation from the International Oil Pollution Compensation Fund (IOPCF) for damage to fishing grounds caused by the Braer tanker spill in January 1993.
The fishermen say that pollution has depleted shellfish stocks and pushed some of them to the brink of bankruptcy.
"The situation is very serious and men are going to lose their boats. Some of them only have days or weeks left," Gary Buchan told Reuters from the boat "Winsome".
Sally Broadley, a spokeswoman for the IOPCF said on Tuesday that the blockade will make no difference to compensation payments.
"They are none the wiser and no further forward," she said.
Broadley said that the shell fishermen had received eight million of the 47 million sterling already paid in compensation to Shetland Islanders following the 85,000 tonne spill.
A further 22 million sterling is being claimed by the fishermen.
"They have claimed such large amounts without any indication of how they arrived at those figures," Broadley said.
Local police boarded the boats on Tuesday morning and gave the fisherman a few hours to leave the harbour.
The boats began to head back to the fishing port of Lerwick at around 1445 GMT, having occupied the oil terminal since 0600 GMT on Monday.
Sullom Voe handles nearly 500,000 barrels per day of crude oil -- about one fifth of Britain's oil output -- and is the export terminal for world benchmark crude Brent blend.
The blockade prevented a fully-loaded tanker from leaving the port on schedule on Tuesday morning and another from berthing in the afternoon.
